reconcile.connective: Defenders resolve the tension by the object of the anger: God's wrath toward his own repentant people is momentary, while toward the impenitent it abides.

discrepancy.connective: Robert G. Ingersoll presses the sharpest form of the objection, arguing that in the Old Testament 'the vengeance of Jehovah stopped at the tomb' and that it was the New Testament that newly introduced the doctrine of eternal pain — so the duration of divine wrath is not one consistent teaching but escalates across the canon.

skeptic.name: Robert G. Ingersoll
skeptic.attribution: Robert G. Ingersoll (d. 1899), Some Reasons Why (1881)

excerpts.excerpt_text: neither will he keep his anger for ever; though he does with the wicked, yet not with his own people; that endures but for a moment, and is rather seeming than real
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly harmonizes both poles of the contradiction: anger 'for ever' is true of the wicked (Jer 17:4 / Mal 1:4 / Matt 25 type), while toward 'his own people' it endures 'but for a moment' (Ps 30:5 / Ps 103:9). The duration depends on the object, not a flat self-contradiction.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-14), on Micah 7:18
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry treats this exact tension on Micah 7:18, distinguishing that God 'will not retain his anger for ever' toward the remnant of his heritage while 'against those that are not of the remnant of his heritage, that are unpardoned, he will keep his anger for ever' — the object-based harmonization keyed to the duration-of-anger question.
